About the podcast

John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).
He cuts through the flummery, misinformation, and plethora of platitudinous pap pushed out by influencers.
In an entertaining format, he sates runners' cravings for knowledge.

John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).
He cuts through the flummery, misinformation, and plethora of platitudinous pap pushed out by influencers.

John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).

Recovery and building back in after a marathon
So this is a really important thing.
Elite athletes don't have a problem taking time off and recovering after marathons, whereas more recreational runners, they struggle to take time off because of their addiction and things like this.
But it's really, really important after a marathon to take, you know, a week to 10 days off and then have a week of easy running and another week of easy running as well.
Because you might feel like you've recovered from a marathon.
But it takes essentially about 3 weeks to recover from a marathon.
And then what you need to do is then transition into some light sessions and start to build your mileage back up.
If you do it this way, the marathon itself works like as a super session and actually will bounce your fitness forward.
If you come off a marathon and start racing straight away, you'll run into trouble.
You're just digging yourself into a hole.
You need to recover.
See people trying to race off the back of marathons as it's not a good idea because you're in marathon fitness, you're not, you're not really in 10K fit fitness.
Some people try to do a few sharpening sessions and then go and race.
But it's much better to take that time off, allow the body to recover, allow the adaptations from the whole block of training, the whole 10 months of training to kick in and it kind of catapults you forward in your fitness.
Yes, you'll be a little bit back on your fitness when you get back into sessions, but after two or three sessions you'll find you'll shoot right forward and move like into a different default form of fitness.
And that's what we did with Eva in November and December so that when she went to Kenya, she was only running 50 miles a week in the middle of December.
And then we just built that up in the time we were in Kenya.
So she was back over 100 miles a week.
We paid attention to the the 10 day rule of not doing anything too serious in the 1st 10 days.
The first week was all easy running out there.
Then a very light session.
There's a 20 minute tempo just to test the ground.
Get used to that as well.

About the podcast
Strava group: https://www.strava.com/clubs
Open Strava Group: https://www.strava.com/clubs/1119827
John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).
He cuts through the flummery, misinformation, and plethora of platitudinous pap pushed out by influencers.
In an entertaining format, he sates runners' cravings for knowledge.
John Starrett

About the podcast

John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).
He cuts through the flummery, misinformation, and plethora of platitudinous pap pushed out by influencers.
In an entertaining format, he sates runners' cravings for knowledge.

Introduction The art of the marathon.
The marathon stands as one of humanity's most profound athletic challenges.
A curious distance of 26.2 miles, 42.195 kilometres that somehow manages to exist at the perfect intersection of achievable and impossible is long enough to humble the fittest athletes, yet accessible enough to beckon ordinary people toward extraordinary accomplishment.
The marathon demands not merely physical fitness that a complex alchemy of physiological preparation, psychological fortitude, tactical wisdom and experiential knowledge that transcends pure science.
In the modern era of wearable technology, exercise Physiology, exercise Physiology, laboratories, biomechanical analysis and evidence based training methodologies, it's become tempting to reduce the marathon preparation to a series of data points and scientific principles.
Heart rate zones replace perceived effort.
Training plans become a logarithms rather than narratives.
Recovery is measured in heart rate variability rather than the subtle language of muscle and mind that experience runners have interpreted for generations.
Science has undoubtedly enriched our understanding of marathon training.
We now comprehend the cellular adaptations that occurred during long runs, the metabolic pathways that govern energy utilisation, and the biomechanical factors that influence running economy.
This knowledge provides valuable tools in the marathon runners arsenal.
Yet tools alone do not create masterpieces, rather it is the skilled hands that wield them.
The limitations of pure science The scientific approach to marathon trainers suffers from several intrinsic limitations.
Research studies typically examine isolated variables under controlled conditions with homogeneous subject groups, conditions entirely unlike the messy interconnected reality of an individual's marathon journey.
The marathon runner is not merely a collection of physiological systems to be optimised, but a whole person embedded within a complex life.
Science excels answering specific, well defined questions.
How does high intensity interval training affect VO2 Max?
What carbohydrate concentration optimises gastric emptying during endurance exercise?
How does footwear influence running the economy?
These are valuable enquiries, but they they examine fragments of a holistic experience.
The more fundamental questions How should this particular runner prepare for their first marathon while balancing family commitments?
How can a veteran marathon runner rediscover joy in training after this appointment?
How might training evolve through different life, life seasons remaining beyond the reach of scientific methodology alone?
Furthermore, scientific knowledge constantly evolves.
Today's certainties become tomorrow's outdated notions.
The runner who anchors their practice entirely in current research risks being perpetually adrift as consensus shifts.
Contrast this with the timeless wisdom accumulated by generations of marathon runners and coaches, knowledge tested not in laboratories but on frost covered tracks in February, wind swept coastal paths in autumn and sun baked roads in high summer.
The Art of the Marathon Coaching Where science reaches its limits, the art of marathon coaching begins to flourish.
This art encompasses several elements that transcend pure scientific knowledge, pattern recognition and intuition.
The masterful coach develops an almost subconscious ability to detect patterns and anomalies in a runner's development.
They notice the slightly altered gait that precedes injury, the subtle shift in demeanour that signals overtraining, or the barely perceptible improvements in form that suggests breakthrough approaches.
This pattern recognition operates too swiftly and integrates too many variables to be reduced to an explicit logarithm.
A coach watching a runner complete intervals might observe dozens of subtle cues simultaneously.
Breathing pattern, facial tension, foot strike, arm carriage, recovery between repetitions, verbal responses, emotional state, and integrate these not and integrate these with knowledge of the runner's recent training history, life circumstances, personality, and previous pattern of adaptation.
From this rich tapestry of information emerges an intuitive judgement.
She could handle one more Rep today, but it would compromise tomorrow's development.
Or his form is beginning to deteriorate in a way that suggests we should reconsider his racing shoes.
Such judgements represent not a rejection of science, but it's transcendence, the integration of explicit scientific knowledge with implicit experiential wisdom in a manner that exceeds what either could achieve alone.
Individualisation as creative practice While science can establish general principles, the art of coaching lies in adapting these principles to the gloriously messy reality of individual human beings.
No2 runners respond identically to the same training stimulus.
Physiological, psychological and circumstantial differences create a unique training fingerprint for each marathon aspirant.
The artful coach approaches each runner as both scientists and artists, drawing upon scientific principles while recognising that their application requires creative interpretation.
Like a master chef who understands food chemistry yet relies on taste and intuition for final seasoning, the masterful marathon coach blends scientific knowledge with experienced judgement to create training programmes tailored to the individual needs.
Consider the challenge of prescribing long runs, the cornerstone of marathon preparation.
Science offers general parameters regarding duration, frequency, and intensity, yet the artful coach must consider countless individual factors.
How does this How does this runner recover from endurance efforts?
What psychological approach works best for their personality?
How do family commitments constrain weekend scheduling?
What routes will provide the appropriate terrain, inspiration and practical support?
The resulting long run strategy becomes not merely scientifically sound, but artfully crafted for the specific runner.

About the podcast

John's one of the most successful online running coaches on the planet. He has a background in journalism and is the founder of Stazza's Stable: a global running community. John coaches a broad range of runners: beginners through elites (national, European, and Olympic standard).
He cuts through the flummery, misinformation, and plethora of platitudinous pap pushed out by influencers.
In an entertaining format, he sates runners' cravings for knowledge.

A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.

About the artist
17,541,215 monthly listeners
A subsidiary of Universal, Republic Records signed the musicians and issued their major-label debut, The Better Life, in early 2000. The Better Life became one of the biggest-selling albums of 2000, going platinum four times during its first year of release and spawning several singles. The band furthered its success with 2002's Away from the Sun, which debuted at number eight on the Billboard Top 200 and, like its predecessor, climbed to multi-platinum status. 3 Doors Down toured steadily throughout 2003 and 2004 in support of Away from the Sun, and issued the live EP Another 700 Miles in November 2003 as a holdover between studio efforts. The group returned with a heavier album, Seventeen Days, in early 2005. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in its first week of release. A self-titled album, which followed in May 2008, repeated its predecessor's success when it too debuted at the top of the Billboard 200. 3 Doors Down toured throughout 2009, released a digital-only acoustic holiday album at the end of the year, and began to work on their next album in 2010. With Howard Benson serving as producer, the guys shuttled themselves between L.A. and Tokyo, recording the album in both cities and eventually emerging with 2011's Time of My Life.
